Intermediate-Rooted

Root Crops
Carrot.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Steady moisture, careful thinning and carrot-fly protection make a big difference. Fresh manure, compaction, stones, drought and rough handling can leave roots forked, tough or damaged.

Quick facts
Sow

Apr – Jun

Harvest

Aug – Oct

Germination

17 days

Depth

1/2 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

early: 8 lb; maincrop: 10 lb

Plant spacing

Thin to 2-3 in. apart

Ready in

Early ~12; maincrop ~16 weeks from sowing

Recommended varieties
SHORT-ROOTED
Early Nantes 2

A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Autumn King

A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Chantenay Red Cored

A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

Key risks
Carrot Fly

Tell-tale signs on carrots are reddish leaves which wilt in sunny weather and later turn yellow.

Fanging

Fanging is usually caused by adding manure or compost to the soil shortly before seed sowing.

Small Roots

Aphids and virus will stunt growth and reduce yield, but even in the absence of pests and diseases many gardeners produce disappointingly small carrots.

Splitting

Much more serious than fanging of carrots, because the roots will not store.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
14

Growing guide · Carrot
Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow thinly

Sow direct, very thinly, in shallow drills.

2 Cover lightly

Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.

3 Thin later

Thin seedlings to the final spacing in Quick facts.

Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist.

Looking after the crop
Thin only as needed in evenings or damp weather; water dry soil first. Firm afterwards and clear thinnings: bruised roots attract carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.
Trim leaves about 1/2 in. above the crown. Store sound roots separately in sand, cool, ventilated and just above freezing; they may keep until March.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Carrot Fly	Tunnelled roots.	Use fine mesh; remove thinnings; avoid bruising.
Fanging	Forked roots	Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.
Small Roots	Small roots; weak growth.	Improve soil; use organic feed if growth is poor.
Splitting	Split roots.	Water evenly; mulch in drought; use split roots now.
Sclerotinia Rot	White mould; rotting roots.	Remove diseased roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Carrot-Willow Aphid	Distorted, stunted leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Black Rot	Black lesions on stored roots.	Remove rotten roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Motley Dwarf Virus	Yellow mottling; red outer leaves.	No cure; remove affected plants. Monitor aphids.
Green Top	Green exposed crowns.	Earth up to cover exposed root tops.
Violet Root Rot	Purple felt-like growth on roots.	Destroy affected roots; never store them; rotate.
Final tips

Avoid fresh manure and disturbance around established roots.

Work from one end of the row when harvesting.

Inspect stored roots and remove any that rot.

fonts.text: Onions and shallots are among the most useful crops in the kitchen garden, providing fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring-planted sets offer a simple start; seed gives a wider choice of colours, sizes and seasonal types. Shallot bulbs usually divide into clusters, while overwintered onions provide earlier harvests. All need clean, fertile ground and careful drying for storage, but differ in timing and bolting risk.
Sow
Feb – Apr; Aug
Harvest
Jun – Sep
Germination
21 days
Seed depth
Row spacing
Between rows: Onions and shallots 12 in.; salad onions 8 in.
Yield (10 ft row)
8 lb
Plant spacing
Between plants: Salad onions 1 in.; single seed-grown onions or shallots 4 in.; onion sets 4–6 in.; onion module clumps 6 in.; shallot sets or module clumps 6–8 in.
Ready in
From planting: sets ~20 weeks, shallots ~18; from sowing: spring ~22, August ~46 weeks
Bright: usual months · Muted: less usual
Bulb Onions
A red onion for salads and cooking, available as seed or sets. Gives the shortlist a clear alternative to brown onions.
Bulb Onions
A familiar brown storage onion, commonly grown from sets. A dependable first choice for a useful household crop.
Bulb Onions
A large, mild onion commonly raised from seed. Useful for generous kitchen bulbs rather than the longest winter storage.
Salad Onions
A familiar salad onion for pulling young. Sow small batches for a steady supply of slender white stems.
Shallots
A copper-skinned shallot normally grown from sets. Its elongated bulbs and good flavour make it a useful kitchen choice.
Shallots
A seed-grown banana shallot with elongated bulbs that are easy to slice. A useful addition to the seed-growing route.
Shallow roots need careful weeding, good drainage and steady moisture.
Only sound, well-ripened bulbs belong in the long-term store.
Choose an open, sunny site with fertile, firm, well-drained soil. Add well-rotted compost before planting; avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen.
Rotate kitchen crops yearly. Rake a fine seedbed for seed-grown onions and test acid soil before liming.
A · From seed
Outdoors: onions March–April; shallots April. Sow thinly, about 5/8 in. deep.
Thin to 2 in., then 4 in. Harden off transplants; plant at their original soil level.
Modules: Sow under cover in late winter. Plant clumps intact: onions 6 in.; shallots 6–8 in. apart.
B · From sets (small bulbs)
Plant in March–April, roots down. Firm and water; protect from birds until rooted.
Onions 4–6 in. apart. Shallots 6–8 in. apart: each set makes a cluster.
Rows: 12 in. apart for bulb onions and shallots.
Salad onions: 1 in. apart; rows 8 in. Overwintering: onion seed late Aug, sets Sep–Oct; shallot sets autumn/winter. Use suitable varieties and well-drained soil.
Weed carefully around shallow roots; water in dry spells and use a thin compost mulch. Replant lifted sets and guard against birds.
Remove flower stems and use bolted bulbs early. Reduce watering as bulbs mature; allow foliage to yellow naturally. Avoid excess nitrogen: thick-necked bulbs store poorly.
Pull salad onions young. Lift mature onions as foliage yellows and falls; lift and separate shallot clusters when ready.

Dry bulbs thoroughly on airy trays, under cover in wet weather. Store sound dry bulbs cool, airy and frost-free; discard rot and use sound damaged or thick-necked bulbs first. Wait until necks and outer skins are dry, often about two weeks.
White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.
Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.
Prolonged cold can trigger premature flowering, especially in large sets or young plants checked by weather.
Leek-moth caterpillars can mine onion and shallot leaves and damage bulbs.
Problem
What to look for
What to do
White Rot (Mouldy Nose)
Yellowing; white mould at roots or base.
Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected ground.
Allium Leaf Miner
White puncture rows; internal larvae or pupae.
Mesh during fly activity; remove infested material.
Bolting
Flower stems develop before bulbs mature.
Use suitable or heat-treated sets; use bolted bulbs early.
Leek Moth
Leaf mines; caterpillars inside.
Remove infested leaves; mesh the rotated bed.
Downy Mildew
Grey mould on leaves; growth is checked.
Remove diseased growth; space well, drain and rotate.
Neck Rot
Stored bulb necks soften with grey mould.
Dry thoroughly; store sound bulbs and remove rots.
Onion Fly
Yellow, drooping leaves; maggots at base.
Remove infested plants; rotate and mesh.
Rust
Orange pustules; leaves may yellow.
Remove badly affected leaves; improve airflow.
Birds Pulling Sets
Newly planted sets are uprooted.
Replant and firm; protect with secure, taut netting.
Bull Neck (Thick Neck)
Thick, fleshy necks dry poorly.
Avoid excess nitrogen; use sound bulbs early.
Unpack delayed sets and spread them in a cool, light place until planting.
Spring sets need suitable soil conditions; prolonged cold increases bolting risk.

Onion Family
Onions and Shallots.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Grow onions and shallots for fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring sets offer a simple start; seed gives more choice of colour, size and season. Shallots usually form clusters; overwintered onions crop earlier. All need clean, fertile ground and thorough drying for storage. Timings and bolting risk vary.

Quick facts
Sow

Feb – Apr; Aug

Harvest

Jun – Sep

Germination

21 days

Seed depth

1.5 cm

Row spacing

Between rows: Onions and shallots 30 cm; salad onions 20 cm

Yield (3 m row)

3.6 kg

Plant spacing

Between plants: Salad onions 2.5 cm; single seed-grown onions or shallots 10 cm; onion sets 10–15 cm; onion module clumps 15 cm; shallot sets or module clumps 15–20 cm

Ready in

From planting: sets ~20 weeks, shallots ~18; from sowing: spring ~22, August ~46 weeks

Recommended varieties
BULB ONIONS
Red Baron

Red bulbs for salads and cooking; available as seed or sets.

BULB ONIONS
Sturon

A dependable brown storage onion, usually grown from sets.

BULB ONIONS
Ailsa Craig

Large, mild bulbs from seed; useful in the kitchen rather than for long winter storage.

SALAD ONIONS
White Lisbon

A familiar salad onion with slender white stems; sow small batches for steady young pickings.

SHALLOTS
Jermor

A flavoursome, copper-skinned shallot with elongated bulbs, usually grown from sets.

SHALLOTS
Zebrune

A banana shallot from seed; elongated bulbs are easy to slice.

Key risks
White Rot (Mouldy Nose)

White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.

Allium Leaf Miner

Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.

Bolting

Prolonged cold can trigger early flowering, especially in large sets or weather-checked young plants.

Leek Moth

Leek-moth caterpillars can mine onion and shallot leaves and damage bulbs.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
68

Growing guide · Onions and Shallots
Start with clean, firm ground.

Weed gently; keep soil drained and evenly moist.

Dry storage bulbs thoroughly.

Long storage needs sound, well-ripened bulbs.

Soil & preparation
Choose open sun and fertile, firm, well-drained soil. Add well-rotted compost before planting; avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen.
Rotate crops yearly. Rake a fine seedbed for sowing; test acid soil before liming.
Looking after the crop
Weed shallow roots carefully; water in dry spells and mulch thinly with compost. Replant lifted sets; guard against birds.
Remove flower stems; use bolted bulbs early. Reduce watering as bulbs mature and let foliage yellow naturally. Excess nitrogen produces thick necks that store poorly.
Harvesting & storage
Pull salad onions young. Lift mature onions when leaves yellow and fall; lift and separate shallot clusters when ready.
Dry on airy trays, covered in wet weather, until necks and outer skins dry: often two weeks. Store sound bulbs cool, airy and frost-free. Discard rot; use sound damaged or thick-necked bulbs first.
Sowing & planting
A · From seed
1 Sow shallowly

Outside: onions March–April; shallots April. Sow thinly, about 1.5 cm deep.

2 Space young plants

Thin to 5 cm, then 10 cm. Harden off transplants; keep their original soil level.

Modules: sow under cover in late winter; plant intact clumps. Spacing: Quick facts.

B · From sets (small bulbs)
1 Plant tip showing

Plant roots down in March–April. Firm, water and guard from birds until rooted.

2 Allow room to grow

Space onions 10–15 cm; shallots 15–20 cm. Each shallot set forms a cluster.

Overwinter: onion seed late Aug, sets Sep–Oct; shallot sets autumn/winter. Suitable varieties, well-drained soil.

Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
White Rot (Mouldy Nose) — Yellow leaves; white mould at roots/base.	Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected soil.
Allium Leaf Miner — White puncture rows; larvae or pupae inside.	Mesh during fly activity; remove infested material.
Bolting — Flower stems before bulbs mature.	Use suitable or heat-treated sets; use bolted bulbs early.
Leek Moth — Leaf mines; caterpillars inside.	Remove infested leaves; mesh rotated beds.
Downy Mildew — Grey leaf mould; stunted growth.	Remove diseased growth; space well, drain and rotate.
Neck Rot — Soft stored necks with grey mould.	Dry well; store sound bulbs; remove rots.
Onion Fly — Yellow, drooping leaves; maggots at base.	Remove infested plants; rotate and mesh.
Rust — Orange pustules; possible yellowing.	Remove badly affected leaves; improve airflow.
Birds Pulling Sets — New sets uprooted.	Replant and firm; use secure, taut netting.
Bull Neck (Thick Neck) — Thick, fleshy necks dry poorly.	Avoid excess nitrogen; use sound bulbs early.
Final tips

Unpack delayed sets and spread them in a cool, light place until planting.

Spring sets need suitable soil conditions; prolonged cold increases bolting risk.
